summary: You implemented a correct brute-force Two Sum solution for standard cases and passed most tests, but missed the platform’s expectation for handling empty/no-solution inputs (return [] instead of raising). You also recognized the optimal hash-map approach but did not implement it, leaving the solution at O(n^2) which is not aligned with the expected performance for n up to 1e5.

test_results.summary_note: Brute-force logic passed basic cases; failed an edge case where empty input should return [] but code raised ValueError.

dimensions.name: Correctness & Completeness
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: Your pair-iteration correctly avoided using the same element twice by starting j from i+1, and it found a valid answer on the standard cases (basic category passed).
dimensions.what_to_improve: Match the required output behavior for edge/no-solution inputs: return [] for empty input (and generally avoid raising) if the environment’s tests include those cases.

dimensions.name: Problem-Solving & Thinking
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: You started with a simple, verifiable baseline (nested loops) and explicitly noted the optimization path (hash map) and key correctness detail (distinct indices).
dimensions.what_to_improve: When prompted about unusual inputs, systematically enumerate boundary conditions (empty list, length 1, no-solution) and reconcile them with constraints vs. test harness expectations before submitting.

dimensions.name: Technical Communication
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: You clearly restated the problem, described the brute-force approach, and gave an accurate complexity assessment when asked.
dimensions.what_to_improve: When constraints say “exactly one valid answer,” explicitly confirm whether the function contract still expects a safe default for invalid/empty input in this platform (e.g., returning []), and state that assumption before coding.

dimensions.name: Complexity & Optimization
dimensions.label: needs work
dimensions.what_went_well: You correctly identified your implemented complexity as O(n^2) time and mentioned the O(n) hash-map alternative.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Implement the canonical single-pass hash map (seen value -> index, check complement before insert) to achieve O(n) time, which is the expected approach for n up to 10^5.

dimensions.name: Code Quality
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: The code is straightforward, readable, and has clear control flow; indices are handled safely (no i==j).
dimensions.what_to_improve: Avoid using exceptions for normal control flow in interview-style problems; return a consistent type (e.g., [] when not found) and consider an early guard like if len(nums) < 2: return [].

dimensions.name: Independence
dimensions.label: needs work
dimensions.what_went_well: You produced a working baseline solution without step-by-step guidance.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Use hints to drive concrete pre-submit checks (run/consider boundary cases) and adapt the solution accordingly; here, the general hint about unusual inputs did not translate into covering the empty-input edge case.

thinking_and_logic: You approached the problem with a brute-force nested-loop search over pairs, ensuring distinct indices by iterating j from i+1. That reasoning is correct for finding a valid pair, but the submission assumed the constraints would always hold in tests and treated no-solution/empty input as exceptional (raising), which conflicted with the test contract that expected an empty list for empty input. You also correctly understood that performance could be improved to O(n) with a hash map but did not transition to that implementation.
code_assessment: Your final code matches the ANSWER KEY’s brute_force approach (nested loops, O(n^2) time, O(1) space) and is logically correct for typical non-empty inputs with a guaranteed solution. Compared to the canonical optimal solution, it misses the single-pass hash map pattern (complement lookup) that reduces runtime from O(n^2) to O(n), which is important under the given constraint of up to 10^5 elements. It also diverges from the listed common pitfall: raising an exception instead of returning an empty result on empty/no-solution inputs, which directly caused the edge test failure.

next_steps.action: Implement the single-pass hash map Two Sum solution (complement check before insert).
next_steps.why: It achieves the expected O(n) time for large inputs and is the canonical interview solution.
next_steps.how: Maintain dict seen = {value: index}; for each i, x in enumerate(nums): if target-x in seen: return [seen[target-x], i]; else seen[x] = i.

next_steps.how: Before submit, mentally test: nums=[], nums length 1, duplicates, negatives, and confirm what to return if not found ([] vs exception) per prompt/tests.

next_steps.action: Practice the sorted-array variant using two pointers.
next_steps.why: It’s a common follow-up and tests whether you can adapt the idea to different constraints (O(n) time, O(1) space).
next_steps.how: With l=0,r=n-1: move l/r based on sum compared to target; return indices when sum==target.

encouragement: You had the core logic and complexity awareness; converting that awareness into the optimal hash-map implementation and doing a quick edge-case contract check would turn this into a fully passing, interview-ready solution.

transcript.text: Here's the problem: given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target.
Let me restate: I need two distinct indices whose values sum to the target. I'll start with the straightforward approach — check every pair with two loops — and optimize if there's time.
Writing the nested loops now. Outer loop i, inner loop from i plus one so I don't reuse the same element.
Okay, it works on the example. Running the visible tests.
Before you finish — consider whether there are any unusual inputs worth checking.
Unusual inputs... duplicates should be fine since I use indices. I think I'm good, submitting.
One of the visible tests failed — the empty input case. You raised an error instead of returning an empty list.
Ah, I see. I assumed there's always a solution because of the constraints, so I raised. I'd need a guard for empty or no-solution inputs.
What's the complexity of your solution?
Two nested loops, so O(n squared) time and constant space. I know a hash map would make it O(n) but I didn't get to it.
